title: API Security
description: Comprehensive security pattern for protecting application programming interfaces across their full lifecycle. Maps 47 NIST 800-53 controls to the critical security functions required to defend APIs against the OWASP API Security Top 10: authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limiting, transport security, inventory management, and continuous monitoring.

metadata.provenance: Derived from securing API-first architectures in financial services, where payment APIs, open banking interfaces, and partner integrations create high-value attack surfaces. Informed by OWASP API Security Top 10, NIST SP 800-204 series on microservices security, and practical experience with API gateways, OAuth 2.0 deployments, and API abuse detection at scale.

contributors.name: Cyber Security Coalition, Enterprise Security Architecture focus group
contributors.contribution: ArchiMate view (threat view and control view), threat-to-control traceability, STRIDE-LM and CAPEC threat classification

previousVersions.note: OSA-only version before the Cyber Security Coalition ArchiMate view was added.

content.description:
Context

APIs are the connective tissue of modern software. Every microservice, mobile app, SaaS integration, partner onboarding flow and IoT device talks through them, so the API surface is now the largest exposed surface most organisations have. Web application firewalls built for rendered pages see only part of it: APIs expose structured data and business logic, and the attacks that matter target authentication, object-level authorisation, data exposure, rate limits and business process abuse.

Summary

API security is four layers on every call. An API gateway authenticates the caller, applies rate limits and validates the request against its schema at the edge. An authorisation layer decides, per object, whether this caller may act on this resource. A validation layer sanitises every input before it reaches business logic. A monitoring layer watches for credential abuse, anomalous usage and data exfiltration. Around the call sits the lifecycle: schema-first design, testing in the pipeline, an inventory of every published API, and deprecation.

The pattern covers that whole lifecycle and applies to REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket and event-driven styles. Its ArchiMate view is narrower on purpose: it draws one inbound call, from a consumer outside the organisation to a service inside it, and shows which control answers which threat at each step. The 32 controls on that path are the architecture; the other 15 come from the organisation around it.

Key principles

Validate at three points, not one. Input is checked at the web application firewall, at the gateway and in the service (SI-10 three times). Teams build one of the three and stop; the service-side check is the one that knows the business rules.

Rate limiting is an identity control too. Network throttling (SC-05) stops floods of requests, but a flood of valid sessions passes it. Session limits and session termination (AC-10, AC-12) at the identity provider stop the second kind.

The API inventory is a security control. An API that is not in the inventory (CM-08) is not behind the gateway, not tested and not monitored. The same inventory is what tells you which third-party APIs you depend on when a supplier is compromised.
keyControlAreas: API Authentication and Identity Management (IA-02, IA-04, IA-05, IA-08, IA-09): Every API call must be authenticated. IA-02 mandates identification and authentication for organisational users accessing APIs, requiring OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens, API keys with HMAC signing, or mutual TLS certificates rather than basic authentication over plain HTTP. IA-04 manages the lifecycle of API credentials: provisioning, rotation, suspension, and revocation of API keys and client IDs. IA-05 governs authenticator management -- token signing key rotation, API key entropy requirements, and credential storage using secrets managers rather than embedded in source code or configuration files. IA-08 extends authentication to non-organisational users: third-party developers, partner integrations, and public API consumers who authenticate via OAuth client credentials, API keys, or federated identity. IA-09 addresses service-to-service authentication -- the critical requirement that internal APIs between microservices use mutual TLS, service mesh identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE), or signed JWTs rather than relying on network-level trust. Implementation requires centralised API key management, short-lived token issuance (15-minute access tokens with refresh rotation), and automated credential rotation with zero-downtime deployment.

API Authorization and Access Control (AC-03, AC-04, AC-06, AC-07, AC-10, AC-12): Authorization in API security must operate at multiple granularities: endpoint level, resource level, field level, and operation level. AC-03 enforces access based on OAuth 2.0 scopes, RBAC roles, or ABAC policies -- critically, authorization must check not just whether the authenticated identity can access the endpoint, but whether it can access the specific resource instance (preventing Broken Object Level Authorization, OWASP API #1). AC-04 controls information flow between API boundaries, preventing APIs from leaking data across trust domains or returning more data than the consumer is authorised to see. AC-06 enforces least privilege: API tokens should carry the minimum scopes required for the specific operation, not blanket admin access. AC-07 limits unsuccessful authentication attempts with progressive rate limiting and account lockout to prevent credential stuffing against API authentication endpoints. AC-10 controls concurrent API sessions to prevent token farming and session multiplication attacks. AC-12 enforces token expiration and session termination -- access tokens must have short lifetimes, refresh tokens must be rotation-bound, and revocation must propagate to all enforcement points within seconds.

API Gateway and Boundary Protection (SC-07, AC-17, AC-20, AC-21): The API gateway is the primary security enforcement point for all API traffic. SC-07 enforces boundary protection: the gateway terminates TLS, validates authentication tokens, applies rate limits, checks schema compliance, and routes only validated requests to backend services. No API consumer should ever communicate directly with backend services -- all traffic flows through the gateway. AC-17 governs remote access to APIs, ensuring that API endpoints exposed to the internet have defence-in-depth controls: WAF integration, DDoS protection, geographic restrictions where appropriate, and IP reputation filtering. AC-20 controls the use of external APIs that the organisation consumes -- third-party API dependencies must be inventoried, risk-assessed, and monitored for availability, security incidents, and breaking changes. AC-21 enables controlled information sharing via APIs while enforcing data classification policies: public endpoints return only public data, partner endpoints enforce contractual data boundaries, and internal endpoints may return richer data but only to authenticated internal services.

Input Validation and Injection Prevention (SI-10, SI-03, SI-11, SI-15): Input validation is the most critical technical control in API security. SI-10 mandates validation of all API input: request parameters, headers, path segments, query strings, and request bodies must be validated against the API schema (OpenAPI, GraphQL schema, protobuf definition) before reaching business logic. This prevents SQL injection, NoSQL injection, command injection, XML external entity attacks, and server-side request forgery. Validation must be allowlist-based (accept known-good) rather than denylist-based (reject known-bad). SI-03 provides malicious code protection at the API layer: scanning uploaded files, detecting encoded payloads, and preventing polyglot attacks that bypass content-type restrictions. SI-11 controls error handling to prevent information leakage -- API error responses must return standardised error codes and messages without exposing stack traces, database schemas, internal paths, or implementation details that aid reconnaissance. SI-15 filters information output to prevent excessive data exposure (OWASP API #3): APIs must return only the fields required by the consumer, implement field-level filtering, and never expose internal identifiers, timestamps, or metadata that the consumer does not need.

Transport Security and Cryptography (SC-08, SC-13, SC-23, SC-28): All API communication must be encrypted in transit and sensitive data encrypted at rest. SC-08 mandates TLS 1.2+ for all API traffic with no fallback to unencrypted HTTP -- this includes internal service-to-service communication, not just external-facing APIs. For service mesh architectures, mutual TLS (mTLS) provides both encryption and service identity verification. SC-13 specifies cryptographic protection for API tokens: JWTs must use asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256, not HS256 with shared secrets), API keys must be generated with sufficient entropy (256-bit minimum), and payload encryption (JWE) should be used for sensitive data in transit. SC-23 ensures session authenticity: API tokens must be bound to the client, protected against replay with short expiration and nonce values, and validated on every request including signature verification, expiration checking, and audience validation. SC-28 protects API data at rest: API logs containing request/response bodies must be encrypted, API key hashes stored rather than plaintext keys, and any API cache or queue containing sensitive data must be encrypted.

API Inventory and Lifecycle Management (CM-02, CM-03, CM-07, CM-08): You cannot secure what you cannot see. CM-08 maintains a real-time inventory of all APIs: every endpoint, version, owner, consumer, authentication method, data classification, and deployment status. Shadow APIs and zombie APIs (deprecated but still accessible) are among the most dangerous attack surfaces. CM-02 establishes baseline configurations for API deployments: standard gateway policies, required security headers (CORS, CSP, HSTS), mandatory TLS versions, and default rate limits. CM-03 controls API changes: schema changes must be versioned, backward-compatible, and deployed through CI/CD with automated contract testing. Breaking changes require consumer notification and migration periods. CM-07 enforces least functionality: disable unused HTTP methods, remove debug endpoints before production deployment, disable GraphQL introspection in production, and decommission deprecated API versions on a published timeline rather than leaving them accessible indefinitely.

API Monitoring and Anomaly Detection (AU-02, AU-03, AU-06, AU-12, CA-07, SI-04): API monitoring must capture both security events and business logic abuse. AU-02 defines auditable API events: all authentication attempts (success and failure), authorisation decisions, rate limit triggers, schema validation failures, and sensitive data access. AU-03 specifies audit record content: timestamp, source IP, authenticated identity, API endpoint, HTTP method, response code, response time, request size, and correlation ID for distributed tracing. AU-06 analyses API audit records to detect patterns: credential stuffing attacks (many failed auths from one IP), broken object level authorization attempts (sequential ID enumeration), data scraping (paginated bulk extraction), and business logic abuse (unusual transaction patterns). AU-12 generates audit records at the API gateway and within backend services, providing end-to-end request tracing. CA-07 provides continuous monitoring of API health, security posture, and compliance. SI-04 monitors API traffic in real-time for anomalies: unusual request volumes, geographic access pattern changes, new user agents, and response size anomalies that may indicate data exfiltration.

API Security Testing and Assessment (CA-02, RA-03, RA-05, SA-08, SA-11): API security must be validated continuously through the development lifecycle. CA-02 provides security assessments of API implementations: penetration testing focused on OWASP API Top 10, fuzzing of all input parameters, and authentication/authorisation bypass testing. RA-03 requires API threat modelling during design: identifying trust boundaries, data flows, authentication points, and potential abuse scenarios before writing code. RA-05 mandates vulnerability scanning: automated DAST tools that test deployed APIs for injection, authentication bypass, and excessive data exposure, integrated into CI/CD pipelines. SA-08 applies security engineering principles to API design: schema-first development with security constraints defined in the API specification, fail-closed authorisation defaults, and defence-in-depth with validation at both gateway and service layers. SA-11 requires developer security testing: unit tests for authorisation logic, contract tests validating schema compliance, and integration tests that verify security controls function correctly across the API stack.
content.assumptions: The organisation develops or consumes APIs as part of its technology stack. An API gateway or reverse proxy capability exists or can be deployed. Development teams follow a schema-first or design-first API development approach (OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, protobuf). OAuth 2.0 or equivalent token-based authentication infrastructure is available. API consumers can be identified and authenticated (even public APIs should require API keys for rate limiting and abuse tracking). A CI/CD pipeline exists for automated testing and deployment. Logging and monitoring infrastructure can ingest and analyse API traffic at the expected volume.
content.typicalChallenges: Legacy APIs that pre-date current security standards resist retrofitting -- they may use basic authentication, lack input validation, or return excessive data in responses. Shadow APIs created by development teams outside governance processes create unknown attack surface. GraphQL APIs with deeply nested queries enable denial-of-service without proper query depth and complexity limits. Versioning strategy disputes slow progress: URL versioning vs header versioning vs content negotiation each have trade-offs. Rate limiting at the right granularity is difficult: too coarse blocks legitimate high-volume consumers, too fine creates operational overhead. API key sprawl across multiple consumers makes rotation and revocation operationally painful without centralised key management. Microservice architectures generate enormous east-west API traffic that is expensive to monitor comprehensively. Documentation drift between API specifications and implementations creates false confidence in security testing. Partner API integrations involve contractual and technical constraints that limit security control options. API deprecation faces resistance when consumers depend on legacy endpoints and migration timelines slip indefinitely.
content.indications: This pattern applies to any organisation that exposes or consumes APIs. It is essential for organisations with public-facing APIs accessed by third-party developers, mobile applications that communicate via REST or GraphQL APIs, microservice architectures with significant service-to-service API traffic, open banking or PSD2 compliance requirements, partner integration programmes with API-based data exchange, IoT device fleets communicating via API endpoints, or any architecture where APIs are the primary interface for data access and business logic execution.
content.contraIndications: This pattern adds unnecessary overhead for purely internal monolithic applications that do not expose APIs. Organisations with exclusively file-based integrations (SFTP, batch processing) may find limited applicability until they modernise to API-based integration. Very early-stage prototypes may defer comprehensive API security controls, though basic authentication and input validation should never be skipped even in prototypes.
content.threatResistance: API Security addresses the OWASP API Security Top 10 and beyond. Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR) is mitigated by resource-level authorization checks at the service layer, not just endpoint-level (AC-03, AC-06). Broken authentication including credential stuffing and API key theft is addressed by strong authenticator management, short-lived tokens, and progressive rate limiting (IA-02, IA-05, AC-07). Excessive data exposure is prevented by field-level output filtering and response schema validation (SI-15, AC-04). Rate limiting bypass and API abuse are controlled by multi-layer throttling at gateway and service levels (AC-07, AC-10, SC-07). Injection attacks through API parameters are blocked by schema-based input validation and allowlist filtering (SI-10, SI-03). Server-side request forgery via API input is prevented by input validation and URL allowlisting (SI-10, SC-07). Mass assignment and parameter tampering are addressed by strict schema validation that rejects unexpected fields (SI-10, AC-03). API supply chain compromise through malicious third-party APIs is mitigated by vendor assessment, monitoring, and circuit-breaker patterns (AC-20, SR-02, SR-03). Man-in-the-middle on API traffic is eliminated by mandatory TLS and certificate pinning for sensitive integrations (SC-08, SC-13). Shadow API exposure is addressed by continuous API inventory and discovery scanning (CM-08, CM-07, RA-05). Token theft and replay attacks are mitigated by short-lived tokens, audience binding, and continuous session validation (SC-23, AC-12, IA-05). API denial of service through resource exhaustion is controlled by rate limiting, query complexity limits, and payload size restrictions (AC-07, SC-07, SI-10).

Public REST API: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE for user-facing APIs, client credentials for server-to-server
API gateway enforcing rate limits (1000 req/min per API key), schema validation against OpenAPI spec, and geographic IP filtering
JWT access tokens with 15-minute expiry, RS256 signing, and audience claim validation on every request
Structured error responses with correlation IDs, no stack traces or internal details in production
Internal Microservices: Service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) with mTLS between all services and SPIFFE identity for service authentication
gRPC with protobuf schema validation, automatic payload size limits, and deadline propagation
Internal API gateway for east-west traffic with circuit breakers, retry budgets, and distributed tracing
Service-to-service authorization via short-lived JWTs issued by internal identity provider
Partner API Integration: Dedicated partner API gateway with per-partner rate limits, IP allowlisting, and webhook signature validation
Contractual data boundaries enforced at the API layer: partner tokens scoped to specific resources and operations
Third-party API dependencies monitored for availability, latency degradation, and security advisories
API versioning with 12-month deprecation windows and automated consumer migration notifications
GraphQL API: Query depth limiting (max 10 levels), query complexity scoring with cost-based rate limiting
Field-level authorization: different user roles see different fields on the same type
Persisted queries in production eliminating arbitrary query execution, introspection disabled
Automatic query complexity analysis in CI/CD preventing deployment of expensive resolver patterns
Developing Areas: GraphQL-specific security tooling is significantly less mature than REST API security tooling. While REST APIs benefit from decades of WAF rules, API gateway policies, and DAST scanners, GraphQL's flexible query language creates novel attack vectors (deeply nested queries, alias-based batching, field suggestion enumeration) that most generic API security tools do not handle. Purpose-built GraphQL security solutions like GraphQL Armor and Stellate are emerging, but enterprise-grade GraphQL security -- including field-level authorization, cost-based rate limiting, and query complexity analysis -- still requires substantial custom implementation.

API abuse detection for business logic attacks is an emerging discipline that sits at the intersection of API security and fraud detection. Traditional API security tools focus on technical attacks (injection, authentication bypass), but the most damaging API attacks increasingly exploit business logic -- inventory manipulation, coupon stacking, price scraping, and competitive intelligence harvesting -- that appear as legitimate API usage at the technical level. Detecting these attacks requires understanding business context and establishing behavioural baselines that current API gateway and WAF products are only beginning to support.

Machine-to-machine API authentication at scale is creating credential management challenges that outpace current tooling. As microservice architectures grow to hundreds or thousands of services, each requiring unique credentials for inter-service communication, the volume of API keys, certificates, and tokens becomes operationally unmanageable with manual processes. Service mesh identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE) and workload identity federation are emerging solutions, but adoption requires significant infrastructure investment and most organisations still manage M2M credentials through a mix of secrets managers and manual processes with inconsistent rotation.

API sprawl discovery -- finding undocumented, shadow, and zombie APIs across the enterprise -- is a rapidly developing market driven by the recognition that organisations typically have 3-5x more APIs than they are aware of. API discovery tools that analyse network traffic, code repositories, and cloud configurations to build comprehensive API inventories are emerging from vendors like Noname Security, Salt Security, and Traceable, but the accuracy of automated discovery varies significantly and maintaining a continuously updated API inventory remains operationally challenging.

Runtime API protection that operates independently of the API gateway is an emerging architectural pattern addressing the limitation that gateway-only security cannot detect or prevent business logic attacks, BOLA, or data exposure that depends on application-level context. Inline and sidecar-based runtime protection solutions inspect API traffic with awareness of the application's data model and authorization logic, but they add latency and complexity that creates tension with the performance requirements of high-throughput API architectures.

references.title: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)
references.note: The definitive list of API security risks. Covers broken authentication, broken authorization (BOLA), excessive data exposure, rate limiting, injection, mass assignment, security misconfiguration, and more. Essential reading for any API security programme.

references.title: NIST SP 800-204: Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems
references.note: NIST guidance on securing microservices architectures including API gateways, service mesh security, and inter-service authentication patterns.

references.title: NIST SP 800-204A: Building Secure Microservices-based Applications Using Service-Mesh Architecture
references.note: Detailed guidance on service mesh security including mTLS, service identity, and API traffic monitoring within microservice deployments.

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: Security and Privacy Controls
references.note: The control catalogue referenced throughout this pattern. Rev 5 controls map directly to API security functions.

references.title: RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
references.note: The foundational specification for API authentication and authorization. Supplemented by RFC 7636 (PKCE), RFC 7519 (JWT), and RFC 8725 (JWT best practices).

references.title: OpenAPI Specification 3.1
references.note: The standard for API description. Schema-first API development using OpenAPI enables automated validation, testing, and documentation generation.

references.title: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide: API Testing
references.note: The API testing chapter of OWASP's Web Security Testing Guide: API reconnaissance, broken object-level and function-level authorization, excessive data exposure, and GraphQL. The guide's other chapters cover authentication, authorization, injection and business logic testing.

references.title: Google API Design Guide
references.note: Google's API design principles including security considerations. Demonstrates production-proven patterns for authentication, error handling, and versioning at scale.

relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-002: SP-002 hardens the servers the API runs on. SP-030 starts at the API interface and assumes the host baseline is in place.
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-004: SP-004 secures the registry where services are published and discovered. SP-030 secures the calls made to them once found, and relies on that registry for its API inventory (CM-08).
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-005: SP-005 covers calls between internal services. SP-030 covers the API as a product exposed to consumers, internal or external, and draws the inbound call from outside in its ArchiMate view.
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-008: SP-008 secures a public web server that renders pages for browsers. SP-030 secures structured data and business logic exposed to programs; where both sit behind the same web application firewall, SP-030 adds the gateway and service-side checks.
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-011: SP-011 sets the shared-responsibility and provider controls for cloud services. SP-030 applies inside that model to any API, whether hosted in the cloud or on premises.
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-016: SP-016 designs the DMZ itself. SP-030 assumes it: the ArchiMate view places the DDoS protection, web application firewall and API gateway in the DMZ zone (NORA-2) that SP-016 defines.
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-028: SP-028 secures the pipeline that builds and ships APIs. SP-030 relies on it for developer testing (SA-11) and dependency integrity, and starts where the API is deployed.
relatedPatternBoundaries.SP-029: SP-029 sets the enterprise zero-trust model: verify every user, device and workload. SP-030 is one application of it to API traffic, including mutual authentication between services (IA-09, SC-23).

threats.name: Broken authentication and credential stuffing
threats.description: An attacker replays leaked username and password pairs, or brute-forces API keys, against the token or login endpoint until one works. APIs are an easy target because they return machine-readable success and failure responses and rarely show a CAPTCHA. The attack lands at the identity provider before any business logic runs. Strong authentication for users and partners (IA-02, IA-08), managed authenticators and identifiers (IA-04, IA-05), lockout on repeated failure (AC-07) and monitoring for spray patterns across accounts (SI-04) answer it.

threats.name: Broken object level authorization (BOLA/IDOR)
threats.description: An authenticated caller changes an object identifier in the path or body, for example /accounts/1043 to /accounts/1044, and the service returns or changes another customer's record. The token is valid, so the gateway lets the call through; only the service knows who owns the object. This is the most common serious API flaw (OWASP API1). Access enforcement per object in the service (AC-03), least privilege on scopes (AC-06), flow enforcement between tenants (AC-04) and review of access patterns (AU-06, SI-04) answer it.

archimate.threat: Unauthorized changes or manipulation of data records

threats.name: Injection attacks via API parameters
threats.description: A caller places SQL, NoSQL, OS command or template syntax in a parameter, header or JSON field, and the service passes it to an interpreter. Schema validation at the gateway catches malformed types but not a well-formed string that carries a payload, which is why validation is needed at the firewall, the gateway and the service (SI-10). Boundary protection (SC-07), malicious content filtering (SI-03), error handling that does not echo internals (SI-11), flow enforcement (AC-04) and monitoring (SI-04) complete the answer.

threats.name: Excessive data exposure in API responses
threats.description: The service returns whole database objects and leaves it to the client to show only some fields, so anyone reading the raw response sees internal identifiers, other users' personal data or security attributes. Unlike object-level authorisation failure, the caller is allowed to see the object, just not every field of it. Field-level output filtering (SI-15), access enforcement and least privilege on the response shape (AC-03, AC-06), flow enforcement (AC-04) and review of response volumes (AU-06, SI-04) answer it.

threats.name: Rate limiting bypass and API abuse
threats.description: A caller works around per-key or per-IP limits by rotating keys, spreading requests across addresses, or opening many valid sessions, then scrapes data or abuses a business function such as a voucher or price check. Each request is legitimate on its own; the abuse is in the volume and the pattern. Network throttling (SC-05, SC-07) is not enough: concurrent session limits and session termination at the identity provider (AC-10, AC-12), lockout (AC-07), event logging (AU-02), resource quotas (SC-06) and behavioural monitoring (SI-04) answer it.

threats.name: Mass assignment and parameter tampering
threats.description: The service binds the request body straight onto an internal object, so a caller who adds a field such as isAdmin or price changes a property the API never meant to expose. It differs from object-level authorisation failure: the caller acts on their own object, but on fields they should not write. Allow-listed input schemas (SI-10), a baseline that defines writable fields (CM-02), secure design of data binding (SA-08), access enforcement and least privilege per field (AC-03, AC-06), flow enforcement (AC-04) and monitoring (SI-04) answer it.

archimate.threat: Unauthorized changes or manipulation of data records

threats.name: Server-side request forgery via API input
threats.description: An API that fetches a URL supplied by the caller, for example to import an image or call a webhook, is pointed at an internal address such as a cloud metadata endpoint or an admin interface. The request leaves from inside the network, so perimeter controls do not see it. The ArchiMate view does not yet name this threat. Validation of target URLs against an allow-list (SI-10), egress restriction at the boundary (SC-07), flow enforcement (AC-04) and content filtering (SI-03) answer it.

threats.name: Third-party API supply chain compromise
threats.description: A third-party API the organisation calls, or a library or SDK used to build the API, is compromised and starts returning malicious data or leaking what it is sent. The organisation's own controls are intact; the trust placed in the supplier is what fails. An inventory of every external API and dependency (CM-08), rules for using external systems (AC-20), authenticating the services called (IA-09), developer testing of dependencies (SA-11), supply chain risk management (SR-02, SR-03) and monitoring of what comes back (SI-04) answer it.

threats.name: Man-in-the-middle on API traffic
threats.description: An attacker positioned on the network path, for example on public Wi-Fi, a compromised proxy or between internal services, reads or alters API traffic, including bearer tokens. Without transport protection a stolen token is as good as a password, and without mutual authentication one service cannot tell another from an impostor. TLS for confidentiality and integrity (SC-08), approved cryptography (SC-13), session authenticity (SC-23) and mutual service authentication (IA-09) answer it.

threats.name: Shadow API and zombie API exposure
threats.description: Teams publish APIs outside the gateway, or old versions keep running after their replacement ships. Nobody tests them, monitors them or patches them, and attackers find them by footprinting hostnames, paths and version numbers. Most organisations have several times more APIs than they think. A maintained API inventory (CM-08), configuration baselines and change control that register new endpoints (CM-02, CM-03), removing unused functionality (CM-07), vulnerability scanning (RA-05) and continuous monitoring (CA-07) answer it.

threats.name: Token theft and replay attacks
threats.description: An attacker steals an access token or refresh token from browser storage, a log file, a mobile app or a network trace, and replays it to act as the user until it expires. The token is genuine, so authentication succeeds. Short-lived tokens and managed authenticators (IA-05), binding the token to the session or client (SC-23), ending sessions on logout, idle time or risk signals (AC-12) and monitoring for one token used from two places (SI-04) answer it.

threats.name: API denial of service via resource exhaustion
threats.description: A caller sends requests that are cheap to make and expensive to answer, such as deeply nested GraphQL queries, huge page sizes or large uploads, until the service or its data store runs out of CPU, memory or connections. It differs from rate-limit abuse in that a handful of requests can be enough. Denial-of-service protection and resource quotas (SC-05, SC-06), query and payload limits enforced at validation (SI-10), boundary protection (SC-07), session limits (AC-07, AC-10, AC-12), event logging (AU-02) and continuous monitoring (CA-07) answer it.

threats.name: Exploit hardware or platform vulnerabilities
threats.description: An attacker exploits a known vulnerability in the platform under the API: the gateway product, the container runtime, the operating system or the firmware of the host. Application-level controls do not help if the layer below them is compromised, and the attacker gains the privileges of the platform. This threat comes from the Cyber Security Coalition's ArchiMate model. Removing unneeded functions and services (CM-07), vulnerability scanning and patching (RA-05) and monitoring for exploitation (SI-04) answer it.

standards: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5, for the control identifiers and titles. Base controls only.
MITRE CAPEC, meta attack patterns, for the threat names.
archimateView.intro: This pattern is available in two notations, and each takes a slightly different angle. The overview gives you a helicopter view of how API security fits into your organisation as a security capability. The ArchiMate view shows the same pattern in ArchiMate notation, and splits it into a threat view, which says what can go wrong, and a control view, which says what we are doing about it. That view should be useful to security architects who work where ArchiMate is the common notation, or to anyone who wants more detail on this pattern.
archimateView.overviewNote:
The overview diagram reads top to bottom in six bands.

  1. Governance, standards and training.
  2. API consumers: web clients, mobile apps, partners and services.
  3. The API security stack: the API gateway, the authorisation layer, validation and protection, and service-to-service mTLS.
  4. Backend services and data.
  5. API lifecycle management.
  6. API monitoring and incident response.

Control identifiers appear as badges beside the block that applies them, and each badge links to that control's page. The legend explains the trust boundary marks. The footer carries the pattern ID and name, the control count, the authors, the status, the date and the standards the pattern addresses.

views.label: What can go wrong (threat view)
views.description:
This view shows one API interaction: a consumer outside the organisation calling a service inside it. It draws the components that take part, the threats that apply at each step, and the controls those threats need. The scope is the inbound call only.

Read the interaction from top to bottom. NORA-1: External holds the API consumer, with a web client, a mobile app and a server-based application inside it. NORA-4: Back Office holds the service and the data store. The call runs from External down to Back Office.

Threats sit in a column beside the zones, each at the height of the step it applies to. Controls follow in the next column, one box each. A control that answers two threats can be drawn twice, once beside each; CM-08 is the only one. A narrow column beside the controls holds the four refinements of SI-10: Allowlisting, Blocklisting, Detailed validation and Data sanitization. The view opens with the controls hidden. Tick Controls to show them, and the view becomes a map from each threat to the controls that answer it.

An arrowhead means the control mitigates the threat it points at, and every mitigation relation has one. A relation running left from a threat to a component means the threat applies there. Every threat also carries a STRIDE-LM category. The view does not draw it. The detail panel beside the diagram shows it when you select a threat.

views.label: What are we doing about it (control view)
views.description:
For every control the threats require, this view shows the security service that delivers it.

The three network zones run down the middle. NORA-1: External holds the API consumer and its three client types. NORA-2: DMZ holds STS-21 distributed denial of service protection, STS-17 web application firewall and STS-23 secure service gateway. NORA-4: Back Office holds the service, the data store and eight more security services. The controls sit left and right of the zones, each beside the service that delivers it. A control appears once for each service that delivers it. The view draws SI-10 three times: at the web application firewall, at the gateway and at the service.

services.STS-13: Security information and event management service
services.STS-21: Distributed denial of service protection service

notes.controls: Every control on the inbound path answers one of the threats in the ArchiMate view. Organisation-level controls are part of the pattern but sit outside the inbound call: governance, training, incident response, at-rest protection and assessment.
notes.typicalChallenges: Three of these challenges appear in the ArchiMate view. Input validation is drawn three times: at the web application firewall, at the gateway and at the service. Teams build one of the three and stop. Rate limiting is not only a network control, because AC-10 and AC-12 sit with the identity provider, and that pair stops a flood of valid sessions. CM-08 answers shadow APIs, and supply chain compromise depends on it too, so an out-of-date inventory of published APIs leaves both threats unanswered.
notes.threatResistance:
The ArchiMate view does not answer one of OSA's threats: server-side request forgery. It is answered by SI-10 and SC-07, already in the pattern, but no threat in the model names it.

The OWASP column uses the 2023 edition of the OWASP API Security Top 10. Injection and adversary in the middle have no entry there, so they show a dash. API3 merges the 2019 entries for excessive data exposure and mass assignment, so two rows carry it.

Two model threats answer two OSA threats each: CAPEC-125: Flooding and Unauthorized changes or manipulation of data records. They should be split in a later version of the model.
notes.assumptions: The ArchiMate view adds two assumptions. The organisation enforces a network zoning model, and the view places every element in External, DMZ or Back Office. The consumer holds a valid access token before the first call reaches the web application firewall. An identity provider validates that token and issues the internal token used behind the gateway. Issuing the first token is outside this pattern.

knownUses: Single-page web application calling an API. The browser holds the token, so session handling carries most of the risk.
Business-to-business API integration. The caller is a server, so IA-09 authenticates the calling service.
Open banking. The consumer is a third party, so AC-20 and the supply chain controls apply.
archimateView.variants: The model records one variant, API IA Threat Model, covering identity and authentication in more detail. No others are known.
